name: Fang (Cameroon)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Mvé, Jean Patrick 2013. Aspects of the phonology of Fáŋ (Lower Fungom, Cameroon; per Glottolog refs; no online copy found)

new_statements.quote: [p.83] Fáŋ happens to be a tone language like most African languages. [...] Moreover, unlike the stress, the tone is carried by a tone bearing unit (TBU) [...] [pp.40-41] the existing long vowels in this language appear solely in penultimate position [...] Mutaka and Tamanji (2000: 38) state that, “allophonic length is sometimes manifested in penultimate position as in Swahioli, Chichewa, Kinande. Length is not contrastive in this position. This penultimate length is interpreted as the manifestation of stress in such languages.” Meanwhile, there are many other words in this language which do not have a penultimate long vowel. We will therefore have to consider these long vowels as marginalized phonemes
new_statements.citation: Mve, Jean Patrick. 2013. Aspects of the phonology of Fáŋ (draft version). MA thesis, Université de Yaoundé I.
new_statements.locator: ch. IV intro, p.83 (PDF p.102); and sec. II-1-2-2 'The phonemic status of long vowels', pp.40-41 (PDF pp.56-57)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fang is described as a tone language with three underlying level tones (L, M, H; surface super-high and contour tones derived). The description contains no rule for word stress or accent. The only prosodic-prominence-adjacent facts given are that (non-contrastive or marginal) vowel length surfaces only in penultimate position of the word (and is lost word-finally), which the author notes is the position where Bantu-type penultimate stress-lengthening occurs elsewhere, without asserting it for Fang; Good et al. 2011:148 independently note the root-initial vowel is sometimes noticeably longer.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule stated); author notes many words lack a penultimate long vowel
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms of isolated nouns and verbs (with class prefix / infinitive ə́-); no phrase-level prosody treated — author explicitly defers prosodic and metrical phonology to future work (p.132).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Fang [fak] of Fang village, Lower Fungom, Menchum Division, NW Region, Cameroon (Glottolog fang1248, Yemne-Kimbi). Good et al. 2011:146 explicitly distinguish it from Fang [fan] (Beti cluster, fang1246) — name overlap coincidental. Mve's consultants were Fang speakers resident in Fang, Wum and Yaoundé. Lovegren 2012 (stem-initial accent) concerns Mungbam (mung1266), a different Lower Fungom language, and must not be transferred to Fang.

sources.locator: ch. IV intro, p.83 (PDF p.102); and sec. II-1-2-2 'The phonemic status of long vowels', pp.40-41 (PDF pp.56-57)
sources.note: Whole thesis is phonology (segments ch.II, syllable/word structure + processes ch.III, tone ch.IV-V: three underlying tones L/M/H plus surface super-high and contours). No section on stress or accent and no statement of where stress falls. Only mentions: p.83 (PDF p.102) 'unlike the stress, the tone is carried by a tone bearing unit'; pp.40-41 (PDF pp.56-57) long vowels occur solely in penultimate position, followed by a Mutaka & Tamanji (2000:38) quotation that penultimate allophonic length is interpreted as stress in Swahili/Chichewa/Kinande-type languages, but the author then treats Fang l…

sources.citation: Good, Jeff, Jesse Lovegren, Jean Patrick Mve, Carine Nguanguep Tchiemouo, Rebecca Voll & Pierpaolo Di Carlo. 2011. The languages of the Lower Fungom region of Cameroon: Grammatical overview. Africana Linguistica 17: 101-164. doi:10.3406/aflin.2011.995
sources.note: Sec. 3.6 Fang (pp.146-152); 3.6.2 Phonology covers consonants, vowels and tones only. p.148: 'noticeable differences in vowel length in surface forms', root-initial vowel of tə̄wésə́ 'culverts' longer, length possibly contrastive; pp.148-149: at least three tone levels plus contours. No word on stress/accent for Fang (the only 'stress' token in the article is 'It should be stressed that...'). PDF itself is altcha-gated on Persée; the saved file is Persée's embedded per-page scanned text layer for pp.101-164.

sources.citation: Lovegren, Jesse. 2012. Stem-initial prominence in Mungbam. In Marlo et al. (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 42nd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 47-54. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla.
sources.note: About neighbouring Mungbam, not Fang: argues the stem-initial syllable carries an abstract accent evidenced only by contrast-distribution asymmetries, 'no overt phonetic correlates of accent have been positively identified'. Areal comparandum only; makes no claim about Fang.

sources.citation: Tschonghongei, Nelson C. & Jeff Good. 2024. Numeral mutation and ablaut in Lower Fungom languages. Afrika und Übersee 97.
sources.note: Four other Lower Fungom varieties; Fang mentioned once in passing; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Nsakse, Ruddygilian Jingkoh. 2022. Lexical variation in Fang and its suggestions for didactic materials: The case of Fang speakers in Souza. MA thesis, University of Buea. 94 pp.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic; pp.21-22 merely summarise Mve 2013 (38 consonants, 11 vowels, 3 underlying tones); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Good, Jeff. 2013. A (micro-)accretion zone in a remnant zone? Lower Fungom in areal-historical perspective. In Bickel, Grenoble, Peterson & Timberlake (eds.), Language typology and historical contingency, 265-282. Amsterdam: Benjamins. (author preprint)
sources.note: Areal-historical overview; Fang cited for prefix loss/consonant mutation in noun classes; no stress or accent content.
